title: Scholarly Certainty Survey and Analysis
author: Mark D D. Wilkinson
license_note: Confirmed via CrossRef DOI metadata: dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.x6nfrde

steps.title: Design and Deploy Certainty Surveys
steps.instruction: Create and administer three distinct surveys (S1, S2, S3) using identical corpora of biomedically-oriented scholarly statements to three comparable groups of researchers with biomedical expertise.

substeps.instruction: For S1: Present 15 randomly selected assertions from the 45-statement corpus; use a 4-point certainty scale (High, Medium High, Medium Low, Low).
For S2: Present 20 randomly selected assertions; use a 2-point certainty scale (Relatively High, Relatively Low).
For S3: Present 20 randomly selected assertions; use a 3-point numerical scale (1, 2, or 3).

For all surveys: Ask participants to indicate the basis of each assertion using a single-answer question with options: Direct Evidence, Indirect Evidence/Reasoning, Speculation, Citation, and I don’t know.

steps.title: Quantify Inter-rater Agreement
steps.instruction: Evaluate the degree of agreement between participants who were presented the same assertion using Holley and Guilford's G Index of agreement.

substeps.instruction: Calculate G using the formula: G = (Probability Observed (Po) - Probability By Chance (Pc)) / (1 - Pc).
Set the a priori chance agreement (Pc) as the inverse of the number of response categories: G=0.25 for S1, G=0.50 for S2, and G=0.33 for S3.
Interpret results based on Landis & Koch thresholds: 0.2 (Poor), 0.21-0.4 (Fair), 0.41-0.60 (Moderate), 0.61-0.80 (Substantial), 0.81-1.00 (Almost Perfect).

steps.title: Analyze Certainty Category Associations
steps.instruction: Investigate the ideal number of clusters for statement grouping based on certainty levels.

substeps.instruction: Perform Hierarchical Clustering analysis (HCA) and the Spearman correlation test to determine certainty category-association between questionnaires, using shared classified statements as the metric.
Generate p-values for Spearman interactions to indicate the existence of correlation.

steps.title: Identify Cluster Patterns and Optimal K
steps.instruction: Apply dimensionality reduction and clustering to identify human behavior patterns across the three survey conditions.

substeps.instruction: Apply Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to the result-sets.
Utilize K-means clustering to identify patterns within the PCA data.
Determine the optimal K (cluster cohesion) by analyzing indices via the R package NbClust (e.g., Gap statistic or Silhouette method) using the majority rule across 30 indices.

steps.title: Evaluate Cluster Membership
steps.instruction: Compare the resulting clusters from the three surveys using the Jaccard similarity index to determine which clusters are most alike via pairwise comparison.
